public_rationale: He said any research from AI 'will absolutely have hallucinations.' On a plain reading, that means every answer. Independent checks by journalists do not bear this out. In the BBC study, 91% of AI answers had at least some issue, which leaves about 9% with no issue of any kind (e1). Also, 19% of answers citing BBC content introduced factual errors, so about 81% did not (e2). A later 22-broadcaster study found major accuracy problems in 20% of answers (e3). These studies show error rates high enough to back his advice to be careful. They also show that many AI answers contain no detected errors, so the universal claim is contradicted.
limitations: If his words are read as rhetorical overstatement ('expect hallucinations'), the evidence would support him.
The evaluations covered news questions, not long deep-research reports.
Reviewers may have missed subtle errors, so the error-free shares could be somewhat lower.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: every answer an AI system gives to a research or fact-finding question contains at least one hallucination, meaning false or fabricated content.

Tested with independent evaluations in which expert reviewers checked AI assistants' answers for factual errors. If a meaningful share of answers had no errors, the universal claim is contradicted. High error rates support the speaker's broader warning but not the universal 'any... absolutely'.

No period was given. The claim is read as describing the AI assistants in public use from 2024 up to the post date (2026-06-15). The checking requirement applies to each whole answer, not to single sentences.
criteria.support_condition: Credible evaluations finding that all, or essentially all, AI research answers contain at least one false or fabricated claim.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evaluations finding that a meaningful share of AI answers to research questions contain no factual errors or issues.

evidence.excerpt: 45% of all AI answers had at least one significant issue, ranging from incorrect source attribution to factual inaccuracies. Source referencing was especially problematic: in 31% of cases, references were missing or misleading, and 20% of responses contained major accuracy issues such as fabricated or outdated information.
evidence.explanation: In a 22-broadcaster study, 20% of answers had major accuracy issues, so most did not. It counts only major issues, so minor errors in the other answers are not ruled out. It also shows high error rates overall.
